reading.body:
Construction AI is measured, not guessed: Census BTOS surveys firms fortnightly, AGC tracks contractor adoption, and BuiltWorlds plus proptech trackers follow the tools, with computer-vision safety monitoring, BIM clash detection, and autonomous site scanning as the working deployments.

The pattern is narrow and physical. The named deployments all watch the jobsite or check a digital model against reality before concrete is poured, so the value is in catching discrepancies early, not in generating designs or schedules. That makes construction AI an on-site perception and verification problem, where the binding constraints are accurate site data and timely action before work proceeds.

What the data does not show is how widely these tools are used, what they save, or how often they fail. It establishes that adoption is tracked through a federal survey, a trade body, a research network, and venture flow, but those sources still reflect firms and startups that choose to report, not the entire industry.

summary: Computer-vision safety monitoring, BIM clash detection, and autonomous site scanning are the working deployments - the sector's AI mostly watches the jobsite and checks the model against reality before concrete is poured.

analysis.body:
The most direct measure of AI use in construction comes from the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which asks firms whether they used AI in the last two weeks. For Construction (NAICS 23) the latest reading is 15.4%, against a prior period of 16.0%. The question was first asked in September 2023, so the series is a short but consistent record rather than a long history, and the Census Bureau notes that S means suppressed where a figure cannot be published. The sourced points describe this as adoption measured rather than guessed, reported directly from firms on a fortnightly basis.

What firms are doing with AI is described mainly by the industry's own networks rather than by measured outcomes. BuiltWorlds, which runs sector intelligence through a membership network for buildings and infrastructure professionals, hosts an annual AI/ML Conference covering the AEC/O industry, with sessions on existing and emerging solutions, use cases across the construction, building and operation process, and strategies for implementation at both project and enterprise levels. Its annual Buildings Conference emphasizes data centers and AI infrastructure. This site's coverage of the sector points to computer-vision safety monitoring, BIM clash detection, and autonomous site scanning as the applications in view, drawn from AGC, BuiltWorlds, and the proptech and contech trackers.

Money and vendors concentrate around the proptech and contech conference circuit. CREtech describes its New York event as a real estate AI conference with 3,000 leaders, 150 speakers, and 20,000+ 1:1 meetings, and says its sessions are led by operators actively deploying AI across their portfolios, with attendees spanning owners, developers, investors, occupiers, construction companies, brokers, and technology leaders. The sourced points note that CREtech and MetaProp track venture flow across architecture, engineering, and construction technology alongside property tech.

Evidence of returns is thin in the harvested material. BuiltWorlds advertises case studies illustrating how companies use specific solutions and the lessons learned from their experiences, and a 2026 AI/ML Conference session titled Quick Wins, Lasting Change: Founders Showcasing AI's Practical Power in Construction. None of the cited pages reports a quantified return, a payback period, or a cost saving from AI, so no such figure can be stated here.

The risks the sources do describe are commercial and labor-related rather than regulatory. AGC, which represents over 27,000 member firms, reports that construction input costs climbed 8.9% between August 2025 and August 2026, and that its survey found war and tariff impacts disrupting projects. The same association reports contractors added 22,000 jobs in August, with the construction unemployment rate hitting a record low of 3.1%, and firms struggling to fill openings. AGC also runs safety and project-executive training, and its sourced description covers technology adoption and safety-technology compliance surveys. None of the cited pages sets out an AI-specific regulatory position for construction.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the picture is a sector where measured use sits at 15.4% of firms, slightly below the prior period's 16.0%, while the surrounding ecosystem of conferences, membership networks, and trackers is far more visible than the deployment data. The applications named, computer-vision safety monitoring, BIM clash detection, and autonomous site scanning, are operational rather than speculative, and the trade body's attention is on cost pressure and labor shortage. What the sources do not supply is proof of return, so a deployment decision has to rest on the firm's own case rather than on published sector evidence.

https://cretech.com/.brief: According to the page, CREtech New York 2026 will be held at the Javits Center in New York City on October 20, 21, 2026, and will bring together 3,000 leaders, 150 speakers, and more than 20,000 pre-scheduled 1:1 meetings. The event is described as a leading real-estate AI conference where sessions are led by operators actively deploying AI in their portfolios, offering real strategy rather than theory. The conference aims to connect owners, developers, investors, occupiers, construction firms, brokers, and tech leaders to discuss AI’s impact on real-estate assets. Tickets are limited, and sponsors and partners are said to represent companies shaping the future of real-estate in the age of AI.

https://www.agc.org/.brief: The Associated General Contractors of America describes offerings for its more than 27,000 member firms, including a safety conference in San Diego and a course for project executives. The association reports that construction input costs rose 8.9% between August 2025 and August 2026, and its survey found war and tariff effects are disrupting projects. It also states contractors added 22,000 jobs in August, with the construction unemployment rate hitting a record low of 3.1%, while firms struggle to fill open positions.

https://builtworlds.com/.brief: BuiltWorlds operates a membership network for buildings and infrastructure professionals. The organization hosts an annual Buildings Conference addressing innovation in building development, design, materials and systems, with particular focus on data centers and AI infrastructure. It also runs an annual AI/ML Conference exploring artificial intelligence and machine learning adoption across the architecture, engineering, construction and operations industry, covering implementation strategies, use cases, and lessons learned from companies deploying these technologies.
